title: Blame-Free Errors: How Error Message Wording Shapes Recovery

Blame-Free Errors: How Error Message Wording Shapes Recovery

Abstract
When a form rejects input, the wording of the error message can either help people recover or make them give up. We report an online experiment (N = 120) in which participants filled in a booking form that rejected their first date entry. The error message was worded in one of three ways: a blaming message ("You entered an invalid date"), a neutral system message ("Date not recognised"), or a constructive message that named the expected format and offered an example ("Use DD.MM.YYYY, for example 07.11.2026"). Recovery on the next attempt rose from 61% (blaming) to 70% (neutral) to 94% (constructive). Blaming wording also lowered self-rated confidence. We argue that the useful part of an error message is the path forward, not the diagnosis.

1 Introduction
Error messages are among the most-read texts in any interface, because people only see them when something has gone wrong and they need to act. Design guidelines have long recommended that messages be polite, precise and constructive. Yet many forms still answer a mistake with a short verdict that places the fault on the user. This paper isolates the wording of a single error message and measures what happens on the next attempt.

2 Background
Nielsen's heuristics ask designers to help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors, and to express messages in plain language. Fictional prior work by Haddad (2022) found that people attribute form errors to themselves even when the system is at fault, which suggests that blaming wording reinforces an existing tendency. A constructive message differs from a neutral one in that it tells people what to do next, typically by stating the expected format or giving an example. A neutral message describes the problem without assigning fault and without a next step.

3 Method
One hundred and twenty adults recruited through an online panel were randomly assigned to one of three wording conditions (40 each). Each participant booked a fictional train ticket. The form was programmed to reject the first date entry regardless of what was typed, so every participant saw the error message exactly once. We recorded whether the second attempt succeeded (recovery), the time to the second attempt, and whether the participant abandoned the form. Afterwards participants rated their confidence in using the form (1-7) and answered one open question about the error. The study took about six minutes.

4 Results
Recovery on the second attempt was 61% with the blaming message, 70% with the neutral message and 94% with the constructive message. Abandonment followed the same order: 18%, 12% and 3%. Time to the second attempt did not differ meaningfully between conditions (median 9-11 s). Confidence ratings were lowest after the blaming message (mean 3.9) and similar after the neutral (5.0) and constructive (5.3) messages.

In the open answers, participants in the blaming condition often wrote that they had "done something stupid", whereas participants in the constructive condition mostly described the format they had to use. Two participants in the neutral condition said they did not know what the system expected and guessed.

5 Discussion and limitations
The largest gain came from adding a next step, not from removing blame: neutral wording improved recovery a little, the example and format improved it a lot. Blame mainly affected how people felt. The study used one form, one kind of error and a single forced mistake, so it says nothing about repeated errors or about errors that are genuinely the user's fault. The sample came from an online panel and the task had no real stakes.

6 Conclusion
Designers should treat an error message as an instruction for the next attempt. Naming the expected format and giving an example made recovery almost certain in our study; avoiding blame protected confidence.

References
Haddad, L. (2022). Who broke the form? Self-blame in data entry. Fictional Journal of Interaction Errors, 4, 33-47.
Nielsen, J. (1994). Enhancing the explanatory power of usability heuristics. Proceedings of CHI 1994, 152-158.
